Elizabeth Clephane
ee-LIZ-uh-beth kluh-FAYN
proper noun
Hebrew Elisheba (“God is an oath” or “God is my fullness”) through the Greek Elizabeth, joined to the Scottish surname Clephane; the name of the frail Scottish poetess of the cross.

Biblical Definition

Elizabeth Cecilia Clephane (1830–1869), a Scotswoman of Melrose in the Borders, was a frail and quiet soul, tender to the poor and afflicted, who gave away nearly all she had to the needy and was called by the villagers “the Sunbeam.” She died at only nine-and-thirty, and most of her hymns were published after her death; yet through her brief life the LORD gave the church two enduring songs. “Beneath the Cross of Jesus” sets the believer in the shadow of “a mighty Rock within a weary land,” content to lose all boast but one: “my glory all the cross.” It is a hymn of penitent adoration before the crucified Lord, tracing every stanza back to Calvary. Her other great hymn, “The Ninety and Nine,” sings the parable of the shepherd who leaves the flock to seek the one lost sheep upon the mountains cold, and who bears it home rejoicing though His own were “shed for one who had gone astray.” Popularized by the singer Ira Sankey in the Moody campaigns, it carried the seeking love of Christ to multitudes. Frail in body, brief in years, and hidden in a Border village, Elizabeth Clephane is honored as a singer of the cross and of the Shepherd’s seeking love.

Webster 1828 Definition

Scottish hymnwriter (1830–1869), author of “Beneath the Cross of Jesus” and “The Ninety and Nine.”

ELIZABETH CLEPHANE, proper noun. Scottish poet and hymnwriter (1830–1869) of Melrose in the Borders.

A frail and generous soul, called “the Sunbeam” for her kindness to the poor and afflicted.

Died at thirty-nine; most of her hymns were published after her death.

Author of “Beneath the Cross of Jesus,” a hymn of adoration before the crucified Lord.

Author of “The Ninety and Nine,” made famous by Ira Sankey in the Moody evangelistic campaigns.

Key Scripture

Luk 15:4 — "What man of you, having an hundred sheep, if he lose one of them, doth not leave the ninety and nine in the wilderness, and go after that which is lost, until he find it?"

Gal 6:14 — "But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom the world is crucified unto me, and I unto the world."

Isa 32:2 — "And a man shall be as an hiding place from the wind, and a covert from the tempest; as rivers of water in a dry place, as the shadow of a great rock in a weary land."

Joh 10:11 — "I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep."

Modern Corruption

A faithful witness, not a contested doctrine; her hymns recover the glory of the cross and the seeking love of the Shepherd.

expand to see more

This entry is preserved to honor a frail and generous woman whose brief, hidden life the LORD made fruitful in song. There is no error to refute, only an example of quiet devotion and a cross-centered praise to commend.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the glory of the cross and the sovereign, seeking love of the Good Shepherd. “I take, O cross, thy shadow for my abiding place; I ask no other sunshine than the sunshine of His face”—such is the settled boast of one who glories in nothing save the cross. Let the church sing of the Shepherd who leaves the ninety and nine to bear the lost one home rejoicing.

Hebrew Roots

The name of a Border poetess whose two hymns exalt the cross and the seeking Shepherd.

expand to see more

Elizabeth — from the Hebrew Elisheba, “God is an oath,” the name of Zacharias’ wife.

Clephane — an old Scottish surname of the Border country where she lived and died.

The parable of Luke 15 supplies the very substance of “The Ninety and Nine.”

Galatians 6:14—“God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross”—is the heart of “Beneath the Cross of Jesus.”

Ira Sankey’s impromptu setting carried “The Ninety and Nine” through the Moody campaigns to multitudes.

Usage

"“Melrose called her ‘the Sunbeam’ for her kindness to the poor.”"

"“We sang ‘Beneath the Cross of Jesus’ and took the cross’s shadow for our abiding place.”"

"“Sankey’s singing of ‘The Ninety and Nine’ moved thousands to the Shepherd who sought them.”"
